newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty seen calmer, yields rising next week.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty seen calmer, yields rising next week.

text.p: The Polish zloty, which has been jumpy for weeks with central bank interventions lurking behind practically every deal, may be in for a smoother ride next week after the bank said on Thursday it was pleased with the current exchange rate.
The National Bank of Poland said it was pleased with the zloty around three percent from the parity rate, which was seen as a warning the central bank would intervene if the zloty gained.

"The central bank statement calmed the market, and the zloty should be around three percent next week, although with a small possibility of an upward test," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA.
Dealers said the zloty could inch higher if large-scale foreign investor purchases of Polish T-bills emerged at Monday's primary tender, but they said such inflows were unlikely.

"If foreigners are active at all, they are likely to bid for small amounts at next Monday's T-bill tender, perhaps in the region of 20 to 30 million zlotys," said Bartlomiej Kumela, treasury dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.
The zloty closed the week at 3.10 percent from the trading band centre, stronger than last Friday's close at 2.80 percent. Next week, it was expected to trade between 2.85-3.15 percent.
Dealers expected yields to continue to edge higher at Monday's one billion zloty T-bill tender amid small demand.

"T-bill yields are not very attractive for Polish banks. And corporate bids, which have driven demand at past auctions, may be curbed by monthly tax payments next week," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Dealers expected investors would bid for about 500 million zlotys at the tender, and average yields should again rise several basis points.
They said the benchmark 52-week paper average yield, last at 20.00 percent, should rise to 20.02, while 26-week bills could break 19.90 from 19.87 percent this coming week.

Dealers said demand would likely be heaviest in the shortest 13-week bills, with that average yield seen rising to around 19.71 from 19.68 percent. In secondary trade on Friday, three month paper was quoted at 19.95/19.80 percent.
The money market was likely to stay liquid for the first part of next week, but dealers said tax payments around February 20 could soak up surplus cash.

"There will be cash on the market next week with perhaps a slight bump in one-day rates later in the week because of tax payments," said Malgorzata Sikora, deposit dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw. "But the rise will not be large."
Overnight rates closed the week around 22.50 percent as clearling house settlement inflows pushed one-day money down from mid-week highs above 23.00 percent.
